1: # Source field definitions
2: 
3: Four files data/*_distances.tsv contain frame_index plus r<resid>_<protein atom>_<ligand atom> columns. Every distance is in Å, computed using nearest periodic image, crosschecked by VMD pbctools wrap + measure bond from the paired deposited PSF/DCD; atom_mapping.tsv gives exact resolved topology indices. tmp and d4tmp filenames encode TMP+ and 4′-DTMP+ bound conditions; wt versus l28r denotes residue28 identity. R28 sidechain columns exist only for L28R. No summaries are provided. Coordinates and unit cells are not mounted; source-card geometric bounds are supplied.
4: 
5: Author Github README assigns these all-atom trajectories to Figure4/6. All four have1001frames if verified metadata agrees. Deposit says1μs; frame0..1000 -> nominal0..1000ns is inferred from duration and count, not independently calibrated by rewritten DCD timestep. Analysis window frame11..1000 implements removal of initial10ns under that mapping. Full-window comparison is optional. The four files are four condition-specific trajectories, not1001 independent replicates. Duplicate210ns simulations mentioned in paper are not this deposit subset.
6: 
7: The operator measures Euclidean heavy-atom distances only, as Figure4. It does not measure angle-qualified hydrogen-bond occupancy, koff, or inhibition rate. Paper hydrogen-bond criterion additionally includes3.2Å and20°; Figure4 average-distance statements have a different role. No discretized state labels are supplied.
8: 
9: experimental_table1.tsv transcribes published Table1 rows (which attribute Ki to ref25), not new laboratory data. Figure3 image is the published duplicate-assay graphic; raw numerical kinetic curves are not provided. Paper.xml is the authoritative full JATS source; paper.md is a searchable XML text derivative whose math/read-order may be incomplete. Verify tables in XML and figures in images when needed.

5: Abstract
6: 
7: Dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) is an important drug target
8: and
9: a highly studied model protein for understanding enzyme dynamics.
10: DHFR’s crucial role in folate synthesis renders it an ideal
11: candidate to understand protein function and protein evolution mechanisms.
12: In this study, to understand how a newly proposed DHFR inhibitor,
13: 4′-deoxy methyl trimethoprim (4′-DTMP), alters evolutionary
14: trajectories, we studied interactions that lead to its superior performance
15: over that of trimethoprim (TMP). To elucidate the inhibition mechanism
16: of 4′-DTMP, we first confirmed, both computationally and experimentally,
17: that the relative binding free energy cost for the mutation of TMP
18: and 4′-DTMP is the same, pointing the origin of the characteristic
19: differences to be kinetic rather than thermodynamic. We then employed
20: an interaction-based analysis by focusing first on the active site
21: and then on the whole enzyme. We confirmed that the polar modification
22: in 4′-DTMP induces additional local interactions with the enzyme,
23: particularly, the M20 loop. These changes are propagated to the whole
24: enzyme as shifts in the hydrogen bond networks. To shed light on the
25: allosteric interactions, we support our analysis with network-based
26: community analysis and show that segmentation of the loop domain of
27: inhibitor-bound DHFR must be avoided by a successful inhibitor.
28: 
29: Received 2023 May 29; Collection date 2023 Aug 14.
30: 
31: Introduction
32: 
33: Antibiotics play a critical role in the
34: treatment and prevention
35: of bacterial infections by inhibiting the growth of these organisms
36: in the host. The discovery of antibiotics has been a breakthrough
37: for mankind by reducing mortality and morbidity from infectious diseases.1 However, antibiotic resistant bacteria have emerged
38: due to the often unnecessary and indiscriminate use of antibiotics;
39: in fact, only a few years may suffice for a new drug to become ineffective
40: in the clinic.2,3 New generation antibiotics are
41: being developed to overcome the resistance problems against existing
42: ones, but bacteria fight back by developing resistance against these
43: new agents.4 Thus, it is of great importance
44: to elucidate the mechanisms that cause resistance and accordingly
45: design drugs that will impede the evolution of resistance.
46: 
47: The
48: design of new and more active drugs based on a knowledge of
49: their mechanism of action plays a central role to overcome antibiotic
50: resistance.5,6 Dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) is an enzyme
51: that has been frequently studied in this framework since it is widely
52: found in all living organisms and has an important role in cell metabolism.7,8 In fact, due to its key biological function, it is an important
53: therapeutic target for anticancer, antimalarial, and antibacterial
54: medicine.9−14 DHFR is necessary for cell growth due to its role in the production
55: of DNA precursors. It catalyzes the reduction of dihydrofolate (DHF)
56: in the presence of the cofactor NADPH to tetrahydrofolate (THF), the
57: precursors for purine and thymine. Escherichia coli DHFR (Figure 1a)
58: has 159 residues and features eight β strands and four α
59: helices, forming an α/β structure arranged into the adenosine
60: binding (ABD) and loop (LD) domains.
61: 
62: DHFR structure, mechanism, and its binding
63: partners studied in
64: this work. a) DHFR structure of the last snapshot of
65: the TMP bound trajectory of the wild type structure, WTTMP. ABD spans residues 38–104, while LD comprises the rest.
66: Loops are identified as M20 (9–24), CD (64–71), FG (116–132),
67: and GH (142–150), whereas the helices are named B (24–36),
68: C (43–51), E (79–86), and F (95–106). b) Schematics of the catalytic reaction of DHFR and its inhibition
69: by TMP. c) Enzyme–substrate interactions. d) TMP and its derivative were studied in this work.
70: 
71: Trimethoprim (TMP, Figure 1b) is a widely used antibiotic compound to
72: treat various bacterial
73: infections.15,16 TMP binds the orthosteric site
74: of DHFR, inhibiting the reduction of DHF to THF (Figure 1b), an essential precursor
75: in the synthesis of nucleic acids.17 The
76: affinity of TMP for bacterial DHFR is much greater than that of the
77: vertebrate enzyme, making this drug highly effective.18 On the other hand, its efficacy is limited due to the TMP
78: resistance acquired by bacteria.19
79: 
80: Pathogenic bacteria can rapidly render antibiotics ineffective
81: through the acquisition of mutations that lead to resistance. Understanding
82: the evolutionary processes of these mutations is of great importance
83: for the discovery of next-generation drugs. Toward this end, it was
84: shown via evolutionary experiments, that it is possible to observe
85: antibiotic resistance emerging in the DHFR encoding gene of bacterial
86: cultures in the laboratory with a device called “morbidostat”.20,21 It was later shown that there was a disproportionate amount of resistant
87: strains carrying the L28R mutation as the first mutation22 and has therefore been used as part of studies
88: for understanding antibiotic resistance.23 Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and biochemical experiments
89: carried out in our group have shown the unique resistance mechanism
90: of the L28R mutant.22,24 The extra hydrogen bonds formed
91: dynamically between the L28R mutant (via residues R52, R57, and especially
92: R28) and the glutamate tail of the DHF substrate lead to an increase
93: in substrate affinity (Figure 1c), thus indirectly leading to TMP resistance. Based on this
94: observation, we hypothesized that a more effective drug could be developed
95: against strains carrying the L28R mutant by making a modification
96: with a polar group at the para and meta positions of the trimethoxybenzene
97: ring of TMP that would induce additional electrostatic and/or hydrogen-bonding
98: interactions (Figure 1d).
99: 
100: Using this rationale, we synthesized an L28R-specific inhibitor
101: by modifying the methyl group at the para (4′) position to
102: a polar hydroxyl group.25 Among several
103: other modifications, this new inhibitor (4′-deoxy trimethoprim;
104: 4′-DTMP) was the only TMP derivative that was effective on
105: both the wild type (WT) and the L28R mutant enzyme. Furthermore, under
106: 4′-DTMP selection, the L28R mutation is largely eliminated,
107: diverting the genetic trajectories to less resistant genotypes. In
108: fact, the derivative exhibited 30–90-fold enhanced antimicrobial
109: activity against isogenic E. coli-L28R compared to
110: native TMP molecule. This study is important in terms of showing that
111: it is possible to impede evolution of antibiotic resistance by blocking
112: plausible evolutionary pathways with the most frequently observed
113: mutant specific inhibitor (see Figure 4c in ref (25)). Therein, TMP-bound WT
114: and L28R structures were also elucidated by X-ray crystallography
115: where TMP is bound to the orthosteric site.25 In another study, we also showed that substrate-enzyme complex (DHF-bound
116: DHFR) is synchronized at the precatalytic step and this behavior is
117: governed by the active site residues which play a gating role, but
118: the effects are propagated to the whole enzyme.26
119: 
120: If utilized to monitor the differences in the dynamics
121: of a protein
122: under varying conditions, MD simulations can inform on not only the
123: thermodynamics but also kinetics of the system.27−29 Therefore,
124: to inspect the mechanistic effects of the inhibitor derivatives, here,
125: we study TMP and 4′-DTMP in the WT and L28R mutant protein
126: environments. Since the binding event is controlled by the hydrogen
127: bonds, we first analyze the orthosteric site interactions for the
128: WT and L28R mutant enzymes for each inhibitor. We supplement these
129: with free energy difference calculations using the free energy perturbation
130: (FEP) method which are also supported by experimental measurements.30,31 We then expand our analysis protein-wide, by inspecting both the
131: hydrogen bond occupancies and the formation of dynamical communities
132: in the residue networks formed in this protein.26,32
133: 
134: Materials and Methods
135: 
136: Parametrization of 4′-DTMP
137: 
138: Trimethoprim derivatives
139: were parametrized using the Force Field ToolKit (ffTK)33 plugin implemented in Visual Molecular Dynamics
140: (VMD).34 The protocol used in our previous
141: study24 to parametrize TMP and TMP+ was followed herein for the TMP derivative. All quantum mechanical
142: calculations necessary for this protocol (optimization of charges,
143: bonds, angles, and dihedrals) were performed by Gaussian09.35
144: 
145: Although it is known that TMP is neutral
146: in water, it may also be in protonated form in the local protein environment
147: depending on the mutant.36 In our previous
148: study, the simulations were conducted in the presence of both neutral
149: and protonated TMP (TMP+), and the protonation state was
150: determined according to the maximum stabilization of the drug in the
151: active site of DHFR.24 Similarly, both
152: neutral and protonated states of 4′-DTMP structures were parametrized
153: in this work, and the resulting parameters are given in Table S1. We find the protonation state of 4′-DTMP
154: to be the same as TMP; i.e., it is protonated when
155: bound both to the WT and to the mutant enzyme according to its hydrogen
156: bonding profile (Figure S1). Therefore,
157: in this study, only results from the protonated forms will be discussed.
158: 
159: System Preparation
160: 
161: All simulations were conducted with
162: the NAMD program.37 The water box was set
163: to the dimensions of 62 × 68 × 60 Å with a padding
164: of 10 Å TIP3P water layer in each direction. The salt concentration
165: was set to isotonic conditions (0.15 M) by using K and Cl ions. The
166: crystal structure was used in the closed conformation (PDB code 6XG5 and 6XG4) as the
167: initial structure,25 and the L28R mutation
168: was introduced using the VMD Mutator Plugin.34 Charmm36 parameter set38 for proteins
169: was utilized. The cofactor NADPH was present in all simulations. The
170: systems were minimized for 10 000 steps. Particle mesh Ewald
171: sum was utilized to calculate long-range electrostatics with a cutoff
172: distance of 12 Å and a switching distance of 10 Å. The RATTLE
173: algorithm was applied, and the Verlet algorithm was used with a time
174: step of 2 fs. The temperature was controlled by Langevin dynamics
175: with a dampening coefficient of 5 ps–1. The pressure
176: was set to 1 atm, and the pressure was regulated by the Langevin piston.
177: The resulting structures were subjected to two 210 ns long production
178: runs as duplicates and a 1 μs long run in the NPT ensemble.
179: As in our previous work, the first 10 ns part of the trajectories
180: was discarded for equilibration. The root mean squared deviation (RMSD)

177: The resulting structures were subjected to two 210 ns long production
178: runs as duplicates and a 1 μs long run in the NPT ensemble.
179: As in our previous work, the first 10 ns part of the trajectories
180: was discarded for equilibration. The root mean squared deviation (RMSD)
181: of the 210 ns-long and 1 μs-long simulations are shown in Figures S2 and S3, respectively. The root mean
182: fluctuation (RMSF) values are reported as averages over all 200 ns
183: long chunks of the trajectories (Figure S4). RMSD values in the equilibrated portion of the trajectories are
184: 1.16 ± 0.19 and 1.28 ± 0.20 for protonated WTTMP trajectories.
185: 
186: Analysis of Hydrogen Bonds
187: 
188: The hydrogen bonds were
189: initially obtained via the Hydrogen Bond plugin implemented in VMD
190: by setting the criteria for the formation of hydrogen bonds with an
191: acceptor–donor heavy atom distance of 3.2 Å and a bond
192: angle of 20°. Hydrogen bonds between the ligand and the protein
193: were extracted using an in-house script that shows neighboring hydrogen
194: bonds of selected residues, and the corresponding distances were
195: calculated using a Tcl script on the TK console of the Visual Molecular
196: Dynamics (VMD) program. For protein wide hydrogen bond occupancies,
197: the method for acquiring hydrogen bonds was used as in ref (26) with an occupancy difference
198: criteria of %20; these were the hydrogens bonds whose occupancies
199: change by more than three standard deviations of the mean (σ
200: = 6.6, Figure S5) which provide the fingerprints
201: of the hydrogen bonds. To select those with significant deviations
202: from the WT, we also calculated errors on these occupancy changes
203: by splitting the 1 μs trajectory into five chunks of 200 ns
204: each. Bonds that show less than 2σ fluctuation were chosen for
205: further refinement (Table S2).
206: 
207: Alchemical Free Energy Perturbation Calculations
208: 
209: Zwanzig’s
210: formulation30 was followed for all the
211: free energy difference calculations. A soft-core potential was introduced
212: to the Lennard-Jones potential by truncating the potential function
213: shifting van der Waals radius 2 Å for reducing singularities
214: occurring during the calculations. Dual topology was used for the
215: TMP+ to 4′-DTMP+ conversions. Initial
216: conformations from seven different time points of the MD simulations
217: were used in sampling to enhance the coverage of the potentially available
218: conformational states. All calculations were carried out with the
219: Charmm36 force field. Particle mesh Ewald sum was employed to control
220: the electrostatics. Langevin piston was used for pressure control.
221: Switching was implemented with a cutoff of 13 Å and a switching
222: distance of 10 Å. The time step was set to 2 fs. The SHAKE algorithm
223: was used for all bonds. Systems were equilibrated for 0.5 ns posterior
224: to 500 steps of minimization. The window size was set to 0.2 ns, 0.1
225: ns being the window for equilibration. The systems were run for 32
226: windows in forward and backward simulations. Acquired results were
227: merged and analyzed by the multistate Bennett-acceptance ratio (MBAR)31 method using the established protocol.39
228: 
229: Dynamical Community Composition
230: 
231: Residue networks (RNs)
232: were built by using a frame for every 10 ns of the last 100 ns part
233: of each trajectory. Cβ (Cα for Glycine)
234: atoms were taken as nodes for the amino acids. C2 atom (Table S1) was used as a node for TMP and 4′-DTMP.
235: Hence, the graphs were constructed with a total number of 160 nodes,
236: and 6.7 cutoff was used to add a link between a pair of nodes. Resulting
237: RNs were undirected and did not have self-loops. Girvan-Newman algorithm40,41 was employed to separate the protein into six communities (Ω
238: = 6) in each snapshot. This algorithm searches for communities by
239: breaking the most central (highest betweenness centrality) edge in
240: each iteration. The calculations were repeated for the equally spaced
241: frames obtained from the MD trajectories. Three well-separated nodes
242: were then selected to visualize the dynamical communities. These represent
243: two locations at the outskirts of each of the LD (N142) and ABD (S64),
244: and one bridging the two domains (I94). Red-green-blue (RGB) scores
245: were accumulated on these three residues such that for each snapshot,
246: if a residue was in the same community as one of these three residues,
247: the color belonging to that residue (I94, N142, and S64 for red, blue,
248: and green, respectively) was incremented by one. Dynamic community
249: composition was then projected on the three-dimensional protein structure
250: by using the normalized (to 256) color score of each residue. For
251: example, if a residue was always in the same community as I94 (RGB
252: value 256,0,0), it was colored red; if another residue was in the
253: same community with I94 and N142 50% of the time each (RGB value 128,0,128),
254: it was colored magenta. See ref (32) for more details.
255: 
256: Protein Overexpression and Purification
257: 
258: The L28R mutation
259: in folA gene was constructed by using the Quick-Change Site-Directed
260: Mutagenesis kit (Stratagene). Six×HisTag was added at the C-termini
261: of the protein sequence for the WT and L28R constructs. The constructs
262: were cloned into expression plasmids pET24a-KanR. BL21 E.
263: coli cells were transformed with pET24a-folA–6×HisTag
264: and were grown overnight in selective media (LB + Kan) and then diluted
265: 100 times into Terrific Broth (TB) media for further growth at 37
266: °C. Protein overexpression was induced when OD600 reached 0.6–0.8,
267: using 250 mM isopropyl β-d-1-thiogalactopyranoside
268: (IPTG) per 1 L of the medium, and the temperature was decreased to
269: 18 °C for overnight growth, with 230 rpm shaking. Recombinant
270: protein was purified using Ni-NTA columns (Qiagen), dialyzed overnight
271: against 50 mM Tris-HCl, 300 mM NaCl, 0.5 mM tris(2-carboxyethyl)phosphine
272: (TCEP), pH 8, and further purified using size-exclusion chromatography.
273: 
274: Steady-State Kinetic Measurements
275: 
276: We followed the protocol
277: outlined in our previous work.22 Briefly,
278: in the DHFR reaction, reactants DHF (Sigma-Aldrich D7006) and NADPH
279: (Sigma-Aldrich N7505) have light absorption at 340 nm wavelength,
280: where the products THF and NADP+ do not absorb light at
281: this wavelength. The reaction concentrations were quantitated using
282: extinction coefficients of 28 mM–1 cm–1 for DHF at 282 nm and 6.22 mM–1 cm–1 for NADPH at 340 nm. The reactions were run in MTEN buffer (50 mM
283: 2-(N-morpholino) ethanesulfonic acid, 25 mM tris
284: base, 25 mM ethanolamine, 100 mM NaCl) pH 7.00, and 5 mM dithiothreitol
285: (DTT, Fisher Scientific BP172-25) was added freshly before starting
286: the reaction. MTEN solution with 150 nM DHFR protein and 200 mM NADPH
287: was prepared. Reaction progression was measured using UV/vis Spectrophotometer
288: (PerkinElmer LAMBDA 650) with 1 s time intervals for two cells. The
289: first cuvette contained the reaction components (DHFR, DHF, and NADPH),
290: and the second cuvette was the reference used for background correction
291: which contained only MTEN and DTT. The reaction concentration for
292: DHF in the first cuvette was 12.5 μM, and the data was collected
293: until DHF was consumed completely, which happens when the curve reaches
294: plateau. To observe the effect of TMP and 4′-DTMP on the reactions,
295: 12.5 μM DHF consumption measurements were used as control. The
296: consumption of 12.5 μM DHF was measured in either WT and L28R
297: mutant in the presence of either TMP or 4′-DTMP. The inhibitor
298: concentration was 500 nM in each case, and all measurements were done
299: in duplicate.
300: 
301: Results and Discussion
302: 
303: Relative Binding Energies Reveal Similar Energetic Cost for
304: 4′-DTMP and TMP Binding to WT and L28R Mutant
305: 
306: 4′-DTMP
307: was designed25 based on our observation
308: that the L28R mutant of DHFR establishes dynamical hydrogen bonds
309: with the substrate DHF in the precatalytic step22,24 and that a TMP derivative exploiting similar dynamics might be effective
310: on both the WT and the mutant enzyme. This observed effect was shown
311: to be of kinetic origin,24 as the free
312: energy difference calculated for binding to WT vs L28R mutants was
313: 1.2 ± 1.4 kcal mol–1 for DHF and 0.6 ±
314: 1.1 kcal mol–1 for TMP. Therein, the calculations
315: were carried out via steered MD simulations. Due to the similarity
316: in the structures of TMP and 4′-DTMP, here we can calculate
317: the thermodynamics of their relative binding with high accuracy using
318: FEP.
319: 
320: The thermodynamic cycle constructed to compute relative
321: free-energy changes due to ligand binding is illustrated in Figure 2. In these cycles,
322: the vertical energy differences (ΔGbind, TMP/4′-DTMPWT/L28R) can be obtained from experimental binding
323: affinities using the relation ΔG = −RT ln Ki (Table 1). The horizontal
324: ones (ΔGTMP→4′-DTMPWT/L28R) are the theoretical values obtained
325: through FEP simulations.
326:

328: thermodynamic cycles
329: of two inhibitors to DHFR. The upper and lower cycles represent the
330: binding of ligands TMP and 4′-DTMP to WT and L28R, respectively.
331: Enzymes are depicted in pacman style, representing WT in light gray
332: and L28R in darker gray. The ligands of each type are represented
333: by burgundy and fuchsia. Throughout the text, we kept the same coloring
334: for TMP (burgundy) and 4′-DTMP (fuchsia). Vertical values are
335: from experiments; horizontal ones are computed. Created with BioRender.com.

345: Experimentally, we find that, while binding to the
346: protein is tighter
347: in the WT than the mutant, they are all in the nanomolar range for

To elucidate the inhibition mechanism 17: of 4′-DTMP, we first confirmed, both computationally and experimentally, 18: that the relative binding free energy cost for the mutation of TMP 19: and 4′-DTMP is the same, pointing the origin of the characteristic 20: differences to be kinetic rather than thermodynamic. 364: Steady-State Kinetic Measurements Point out an Inhibitory Difference
365: for TMP and 4′-DTMP

367: In kinetic assays, we measured
368: the consumption of DHF in the absence and presence of the inhibitors
369: (Figure 3). The initial

371: for WT and L28R mutant enzymes. DHF was consumed in 30 s in control

373: nM TMP and 4′-DTMP molecules were added, we did not observe

376: the other hand, in the DHF consumption control experiment for the
377: L28R mutant, we observed a slower trend continuing for a few minutes.
378: Since WT protein is optimized for the environmental conditions, the
379: slower reaction kinetics for L28R is expected; in fact, the more resistant
380: mutants of bacteria are likely to grow slower than WT, introducing
381: a resistance cost.42 When 500 nM inhibitors
382: are added to the mutants, both are able to introduce a slowing down
383: in product release, more so for 4′-DTMP than for TMP. Thus,
384: the slight edge introduced by 4′-DTMP on the L28R mutant finds

386: interactions in the dynamics of inhibitor bound DHFR to illuminate

396: Hydrogen Bond Occupancies Differentiate Binding Modes of the
397: Two Inhibitors
398: 
399: To elucidate the mechanism of binding of the
400: new inhibitor and thus to highlight the interactions responsible for
401: its enzymatic activity, a detailed hydrogen bond analysis in the WT
402: and L28R mutant of E. coli DHFR
403: with TMP derivatives has been conducted by analyzing the MD simulations
404: for each system.

406: In the crystal structure of WTTMP and L28RTMP (PDB codes 6XG5 and 6XG4(25)), the pyrimidine
407: ring of TMP is stabilized by the backbone oxygen atoms of I5 and I94
408: and the side chains of D27, Y100, and T113, whereas the trimethoxybenzene
409: ring is stabilized via the side chain of S49 (also see Figure S1). We monitored the average hydrogen
410: bond distances in the WT and the L28R mutant in the presence of TMP
411: and its derivative 4′-DTMP. The hydrogen bonds established
412: between the 2,4-diamino pyrimidine ring of the ligand and the active
413: site residues of the protein are highly conserved, contributing to
414: the stabilization of the ligand within the active site of DHFR (Figure S1). While the pyrimidine ring of the
415: ligand is stabilized with strong hydrogen bonds both in WT and in
416: L28R, we observe a dynamic stabilization of the trimethoxybenzene
417: ring of the ligand. Residues N18, M20, W22, D27, S49, and R52 come
418: in proximity occasionally and sometimes lose their contact resulting
419: in larger average values for the contacts determining hydrogen bond
420: distances. In particular, N18, M20, and W22 show significant changes
421: in hydrogen bonding distances in both WT and L28R for 4′-DTMP
422: (Figure 4a). On the
423: other hand, for the L28R mutant, the most fundamental difference is
424: the interactions of oxygen atoms at the 4′ and 5′ positions
425: on the inhibitors with the R28 atoms whereby frequent strong interactions
426: are formed with 4′-DTMP, which do not form with TMP (Figure 4b).
